## Intractability of Exact Inference

For standard single-layer GPs, the posterior $p(f_* \mid \vX, \vy)$ and marginal likelihood $p(\vy \mid \vX)$ give closed-form expressions due to Gaussian conjugacy [@rasmussen_gaussian_2008]. In DGPs this is lost because composition of GPs produces a non-Gaussian joint distribution.

The marginal likelihood requires integrating out all latent functions:

$$
p(\vy \mid \vX) = \int p(\vy \mid \vF^{(L)}) \prod_{\ell=1}^{L} p(\vF^{(\ell)} \mid \vF^{(\ell-1)}) \, d\vF^{(1)} \cdots d\vF^{(L)},
$$

where $\vF^{(0)} = \vX$. This integral has no closed-form solution for $L \geq 2$ (unless the kernel is linear, which reduces the composition to a single-layer GP). The fundamental obstacle is that the covariance matrix $K^{(\ell)}$ at each layer is a nonlinear function of $\vF^{(\ell-1)}$. This is the very variables being integrated over and so the integral cannot be reorganised into the product-of-Gaussians form that makes single-layer GP inference tractable.

To see why, consider a two-layer DGP. The covariance matrix $K^{(2)}$ depends on $\vF^{(1)}$ through $[K^{(2)}]_{ij} = k^{(2)}(f_i^{(1)}, f_j^{(1)})$. For the squared exponential kernel:

$$
k^{(2)}(h_1, h_2) = \sigma_f^2 \exp\left(-\frac{(h_1 - h_2)^2}{2\ell^2}\right),
$$

this is a nonlinear function of the Gaussian random variables $(f_i^{(1)}, f_j^{(1)})$. The integral

$$
\int \mathcal{N}(\vF^{(2)} \mid \vzero, K^{(2)}(\vF^{(1)})) \mathcal{N}(\vF^{(1)} \mid \vzero, K^{(1)}) \, d\vF^{(1)}
$$

is a mixture of Gaussians with continuously varying covariance. Intuitively, for every possible realisation of $\vF^{(1)}$ there is a different Gaussian over $\vF^{(2)}$; marginalising out $\vF^{(1)}$ means averaging together infinitely many Gaussians with different shapes, producing a result that is heavier-tailed and more complex than any individual Gaussian component. These do not have a closed-form expression, and the resulting distribution over $\vF^{(2)}$ is non-Gaussian.

As well as the intractability of the marginal likelihood, the resulting joint distribution over the final-layer latent values is non-Gaussian. Consider a two-layer DGP with first-layer outputs $h_1 = f^{(1)}(x_1)$, $h_2 = f^{(1)}(x_2)$. From the GP prior:

$$
\begin{bmatrix} h_1 \\ h_2 \end{bmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\vzero, \begin{bmatrix} k^{(1)}_{11} & k^{(1)}_{12} \\ k^{(1)}_{12} & k^{(1)}_{22} \end{bmatrix}\right).
$$

Writing $f_i^{(2)} = f^{(2)}(h_i)$ for the second-layer latent at input $h_i$, conditioning on $(h_1, h_2)$ gives:

$$
\begin{bmatrix} f_1^{(2)} \\ f_2^{(2)} \end{bmatrix} \Bigg| h_1, h_2 \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\vzero, \begin{bmatrix} k^{(2)}(h_1, h_1) & k^{(2)}(h_1, h_2) \\ k^{(2)}(h_1, h_2) & k^{(2)}(h_2, h_2) \end{bmatrix}\right).
$$

The marginal distribution

$$
p(f_1^{(2)}, f_2^{(2)}) = \int p(f_1^{(2)}, f_2^{(2)} \mid h_1, h_2) \, p(h_1, h_2) \, dh_1 \, dh_2
$$

is a continuous mixture of Gaussians with varying covariance matrices. Since $k^{(2)}(h_1, h_2)$ is a nonlinear function of $(h_1, h_2)$, this mixture is not Gaussian, so the output $\vy = \vf^{(2)} + \vepsilon$ is also non-Gaussian.

The posterior over all latent functions is:

$$
p(\vF^{(1:L)} \mid \vX, \vy) = \frac{p(\vy \mid \vF^{(L)}) \prod_{\ell=1}^{L} p(\vF^{(\ell)} \mid \vF^{(\ell-1)})}{p(\vy \mid \vX)}.
$$

Since both the numerator (a product of coupled Gaussians) and the denominator (the intractable marginal likelihood) lack closed forms, exact posterior computation is infeasible.

Even numerical integration is impractical. The integration is over $\sum_{\ell=1}^{L} n d_\ell$ continuous variables, which cannot be factored across layers due to kernel dependencies. This motivates the development of approximate inference methods for DGP learning [@damianou_deep_2013; @salimbeni_doubly_2017].
